questions.title: Motor supply of the intrinsic laryngeal muscles
questions.question: Innervation of the intrinsic muscles of the larynx comes mainly from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The superior laryngeal nerve's external branch supplies only the cricothyroid muscle, and its internal branch is sensory to the supraglottis; it does not supply the other intrinsic muscles.
explanations.B: Correct. The recurrent laryngeal nerve is the motor nerve of all the intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid. It also carries sensation from below the vocal cords. Injury to it therefore paralyses cord movement and changes the voice.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies the pharynx and posterior third of the tongue, not the intrinsic laryngeal muscles.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The hypoglossal nerve is the motor nerve of the tongue muscles and has no role in laryngeal muscle innervation.

questions.learning_objective: State that the recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies the intrinsic laryngeal muscles (except cricothyroid).

questions.title: Muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve
questions.question: The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all the muscles of the larynx EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The interarytenoid is an intrinsic laryngeal muscle supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Correct. The cricothyroid is the one intrinsic laryngeal muscle NOT supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve; it is supplied by the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve. It tenses the vocal cords, so a superior laryngeal palsy weakens and lowers the voice. Every other intrinsic laryngeal muscle receives the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The thyrohyoid is not an intrinsic laryngeal muscle at all — it is an infrahyoid strap muscle supplied by the C1 fibres running with the hypoglossal nerve, so it lies outside the intrinsic-muscle group the stem is asking about.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior cricoarytenoid, the sole abductor of the vocal cords, is supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The lateral cricoarytenoid is an adductor supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the cricothyroid as the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle not supplied by the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

questions.title: Correct statement about laryngomalacia
questions.question: Choose the correct statement regarding laryngomalacia:

options.A: It starts in infancy and persists till adulthood.
options.B: There is hoarseness of voice in all cases.
options.C: Stridor decreases on lying on the back and increases on lying on the face.
options.D: Most cases need only observation as the condition resolves spontaneously.
options.E: It frequently needs an artificial airway with tracheostomy or endotracheal intubation.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Laryngomalacia appears in the first weeks of life and typically resolves by 18-24 months as the laryngeal cartilage stiffens; it does not persist into adulthood.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The voice and cry are characteristically normal because the vocal cords are not involved, so hoarseness in every case is untrue.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The stridor of laryngomalacia is worse when the infant lies supine (on the back) and improves in the prone position, the opposite of what this option states.
explanations.D: Correct. Laryngomalacia is a self-limiting congenital softening of the supraglottic cartilages, and the great majority of infants need only reassurance and observation because it resolves spontaneously as the larynx matures. Surgery (supraglottoplasty) is reserved for the few with failure to thrive or severe obstruction. It is the commonest congenital cause of stridor.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Only a small minority with severe obstruction or feeding failure need airway intervention; most never require tracheostomy or intubation.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise laryngomalacia as a self-limiting condition that usually needs only observation.

questions.title: Infant stridor with a hoarse cry — the unlikely diagnosis
questions.question: An infant is noticed to have stridor and a hoarse cry. All of the following diagnoses are possible EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A laryngeal web lies at the level of the vocal cords and produces both stridor and an abnormal (hoarse or weak) cry, so it fits the picture.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Congenital laryngeal (vocal cord) paralysis affects cord movement and causes both stridor and a hoarse or weak cry.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A congenital laryngeal cyst can obstruct the airway and distort the cords, giving stridor together with a hoarse cry.
explanations.D: Correct. Laryngomalacia is the exception because it is a supraglottic disorder that spares the vocal cords, so the cry and voice are normal even though the infant has inspiratory stridor. A hoarse cry points instead to a lesion at cord level (web, paralysis or cyst). A normal voice with stridor is what suggests laryngomalacia.

questions.learning_objective: Use the normal voice of laryngomalacia to distinguish it from cord-level causes of infant stridor.

questions.title: False statement about laryngomalacia
questions.question: All of the following are correct about laryngomalacia EXCEPT:

options.A: It is due to a congenitally weak, flaccid larynx.
options.D: Inspiratory stridor starts soon after birth.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Laryngomalacia is due to a congenitally soft, flaccid supraglottic framework that collapses on inspiration, so this statement is true.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The infant is otherwise healthy and thriving in typical laryngomalacia, so this is a true statement rather than the exception.
explanations.C: Correct. Laryngomalacia affects the supraglottic structures (the omega-shaped epiglottis, short aryepiglottic folds and bulky arytenoids), NOT the vocal cords, which is why the voice is normal. Saying it affects the vocal cords is therefore the false statement. Disease at cord level would instead alter the cry.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Inspiratory stridor beginning within the first weeks of life is characteristic, so this statement is true.

questions.learning_objective: State that laryngomalacia affects the supraglottis and spares the vocal cords.

questions.title: Clues to an inhaled foreign body in a child
questions.question: Which of the following raises the suspicion of an inhaled foreign body in a young child?

options.A: A history of a sudden attack of cough, choking and cyanosis.
options.B: A chest X-ray showing unilateral lung emphysema.
options.C: A chest X-ray showing unilateral lung atelectasis.

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer. A witnessed choking crisis strongly suggests an inhaled foreign body, but it is only one of several clues listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer. A ball-valve foreign body traps air distally and produces unilateral obstructive emphysema — a real sign, but not the only one.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer. Complete bronchial obstruction instead collapses that lung (unilateral atelectasis); this too is only one of the listed features.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single answer. Persistent wheeze localised to one lung is a classic sign of a bronchial foreign body, but again only one of several clues.
explanations.E: Correct. All the listed features — a sudden choking, coughing and cyanotic attack, unilateral emphysema or atelectasis on the chest film, and persistent unilateral wheeze — raise the suspicion of an inhaled foreign body. Any of them in a young child mandates bronchoscopy. That is why 'all of the above' is the answer.

questions.learning_objective: List the history and chest X-ray clues that suggest an inhaled foreign body.

questions.title: Toddler with sudden respiratory distress and cyanosis
questions.question: A 3-year-old boy has sudden acute respiratory distress with spasmodic cough, cyanosis and use of the accessory respiratory muscles. This is most probably due to:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute follicular tonsillitis causes sore throat, fever and dysphagia, not a sudden choking attack with cyanosis.
explanations.B: Correct. A sudden attack of spasmodic cough, cyanosis and respiratory distress with accessory-muscle use in a toddler is the classic presentation of an inhaled foreign body. Children of this age explore with the mouth and readily aspirate nuts or small objects. Urgent bronchoscopy for removal is required.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Adenoid hypertrophy causes gradual nasal obstruction, snoring and mouth-breathing, not an acute choking crisis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A vocal cord nodule causes chronic hoarseness from voice abuse, not sudden respiratory distress.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise the sudden choking presentation of an inhaled foreign body in a toddler.

questions.title: Commonest site an inhaled foreign body lodges
questions.question: An inhaled foreign body is more commonly lodged in the:

options.C: Right or left main bronchi equally

explanations.A: Correct. An inhaled foreign body most often lodges in the RIGHT main bronchus because it is wider, shorter and more vertical (more in line with the trachea) than the left. Aspirated material therefore tends to travel down the right side. The same anatomy explains right-sided aspiration pneumonia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The left main bronchus is narrower and more horizontal, so it receives aspirated objects less often than the right.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Although a foreign body can occasionally enter either side, the question asks for the commonest site, which is specifically the right.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Large objects may impact at the larynx, but small inhaled foreign bodies usually pass through to a main bronchus, the right one most often.

questions.learning_objective: State that an inhaled foreign body most commonly lodges in the right main bronchus and explain why.

questions.title: Premalignant benign laryngeal lesion
questions.question: Which of the following benign lesions of the larynx can be pre-cancerous?

explanations.A: Correct. Laryngeal leukoplakia is a white keratotic patch of the vocal cord, driven by smoking, and it carries epithelial dysplasia that can progress to squamous cell carcinoma. It is the classic premalignant lesion of the larynx and must be biopsied and followed up. Stopping smoking is essential.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Reinke's oedema (polypoid cord swelling from smoking and voice abuse) causes a deep, hoarse voice but is not itself premalignant.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A laryngeal (singer's) nodule is a benign response to voice abuse with no malignant potential.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Laryngosclerosis (laryngoscleroma) is a chronic granulomatous infection; it causes stenosis, not malignant transformation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis is generally benign and only rarely undergoes malignant change, so among these options leukoplakia is the established premalignant lesion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify leukoplakia as the premalignant benign lesion of the larynx.

questions.hold: Non-unique positive stem. 'Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis:' is keyed d (occurs in children), but recurrent respiratory papillomatosis has both a juvenile form (children) AND an adult-onset form (option a, occurs in adults), and malignant transformation is a recognised event (option b, may turn malignant). At least two of the four statements are defensible, so the key is not uniquely correct. Held per the never-guess rule.

questions.title: Investigation not used for cancer larynx
questions.question: Investigations for cancer of the larynx include all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: CT scan to assess tumour extension and lymph node involvement.
options.B: Biopsy by direct laryngoscopy to confirm the diagnosis.
options.C: Metastatic work-up: chest X-ray, brain CT scan, bone scan and abdominal ultrasound.

explanations.A: Incorrect. CT of the neck is routine to map tumour extension and nodal disease, so it is a genuine investigation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Biopsy taken at direct laryngoscopy provides the tissue diagnosis and is essential, so it is not the exception.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A metastatic work-up is part of staging, so it is a real investigation rather than the exception.
explanations.D: Correct. Carotid angiography and embolization is a vascular interventional procedure used for highly vascular tumours such as juvenile angiofibroma or paragangliomas, NOT part of the routine work-up of laryngeal carcinoma. It is therefore the exception. Laryngeal cancer is assessed by endoscopy and biopsy, CT or MRI, and a metastatic survey.

questions.learning_objective: List the investigations used to stage laryngeal carcinoma and recognise which is not part of the work-up.

questions.title: True statement about glottic carcinoma
questions.question: Regarding glottic laryngeal carcinoma, which is the true statement?

options.A: Hoarseness of voice is an early presentation.
options.B: Dysphagia and regurgitation are early common symptoms.
options.C: It usually presents in late stages.

explanations.A: Correct. A glottic (vocal cord) carcinoma disturbs cord vibration from the outset, so progressive hoarseness is an early symptom that brings the patient to attention while the tumour is still small. This early warning, together with the sparse lymphatic drainage of the glottis, gives glottic cancer a relatively good prognosis. Any hoarseness lasting more than 2-3 weeks in a smoker needs laryngoscopy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dysphagia and regurgitation are features of hypopharyngeal or advanced supraglottic disease, not of early glottic cancer.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Because hoarseness appears early, glottic carcinoma is usually detected at an early stage rather than late.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The glottis has a poor lymphatic supply, so nodal metastasis is late, not early.

questions.learning_objective: State that glottic carcinoma presents early with hoarseness and has a good prognosis.

questions.title: Treatment of advanced node-positive cancer larynx
questions.question: The treatment of advanced cancer of the larynx with neck lymph node metastasis is:

options.C: Total laryngectomy and radical neck dissection.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Partial laryngectomy is a conservation option for selected early tumours, not for advanced disease with nodal spread.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Antibiotics have no role in treating a laryngeal malignancy.
explanations.C: Correct. Advanced laryngeal carcinoma with palpable neck node metastasis is treated by total laryngectomy together with neck dissection (with adjuvant radiotherapy), removing both the primary and the nodal disease. Organ-preservation chemoradiation is an alternative in some protocols, but among these options this is the definitive surgical answer. Voice rehabilitation follows total laryngectomy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Laser cordectomy treats only very early, cord-confined tumours, not advanced node-positive disease.

questions.learning_objective: State that advanced node-positive laryngeal cancer is treated by total laryngectomy and neck dissection.

questions.title: Features of the single (adult) laryngeal papilloma
questions.question: The single laryngeal papilloma of the adult:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer. A single (solitary) laryngeal papilloma is typical of adults, but this is only one true feature.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer. Sitting usually on the vocal cord, it causes hoarseness — true, but not the whole answer.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer. It is removed by microlaryngosurgery (with biopsy), which is correct but only one of the features.
explanations.D: Incorrect as the single answer. The adult solitary papilloma is regarded as premalignant and can undergo malignant change — again only one of the listed truths.
explanations.E: Correct. The adult single laryngeal papilloma occurs in adults, presents with hoarseness, is treated by microlaryngeal excision, and is premalignant (may turn malignant), so all the statements are correct. This contrasts with juvenile multiple papillomatosis, which tends to regress at puberty and rarely turns malignant. Hence 'all of the above'.

questions.learning_objective: List the features of the adult single laryngeal papilloma, including its premalignant potential.

questions.title: Meaning of T3 in cancer larynx
questions.question: T3 cancer of the larynx means:

options.C: Multiple ipsilateral neck lymph nodes, each less than 6 cm.
options.D: Tumour involving two regions of the larynx.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Spread beyond the larynx (for example through the thyroid cartilage into neck tissues) is T4, not T3.
explanations.B: Correct. In laryngeal cancer T-staging, T3 denotes a tumour still confined to the larynx but with vocal cord FIXATION (and/or invasion of the paraglottic space or the inner cortex of the thyroid cartilage). Fixation signals deep muscle or space involvement while the tumour remains intralaryngeal. T4 is reserved for cartilage penetration or extralaryngeal spread.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Multiple ipsilateral nodes each under 6 cm describe the N stage (N2b), not the T stage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Involving two subsites relates to tumour extent, but the defining feature of T3 is cord fixation, not merely spanning two regions.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A correct definition is offered (fixed vocal cord), so 'none of the above' is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: Define T3 laryngeal carcinoma as vocal cord fixation with the tumour still intralaryngeal.

questions.title: Child with warty growths on both vocal cords
questions.question: A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with stridor. He has had hoarseness of voice for a year. His temperature is 37 degrees C, and nasal and oral examination show no disease. Laryngeal examination shows warty growths affecting both vocal cords and reducing the airway. The most likely diagnosis is:

options.E: Chronic laryngitis secondary to gastro-oesophageal reflux

explanations.A: Correct. Warty (papillomatous) growths on both vocal cords in a child, with a year of hoarseness now progressing to stridor, are characteristic of juvenile-onset recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (caused by HPV types 6 and 11). The lesions are multiple, recur after removal, and can obstruct the airway. Treatment is repeated microlaryngeal or laser excision to keep the airway clear.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vocal cord nodules are small, smooth, symmetrical swellings from voice abuse, not warty growths, and they do not cause stridor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Laryngoscleroma is a chronic granuloma causing subglottic stenosis, not warty cord lesions in a young child.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Laryngomalacia presents in infancy with stridor and a normal voice, not warty cord growths with a year of hoarseness.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Reflux laryngitis causes posterior cord inflammation and hoarseness, not discrete warty growths.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise juvenile recurrent respiratory papillomatosis from warty growths on both vocal cords in a child.

questions.title: False statement about laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma
questions.question: Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma is characterized by all of the following EXCEPT:

options.A: Smoking is a predisposing factor in carcinogenesis.
options.B: It seldom arises from the subglottic area.
options.C: Invasion of the laryngeal cartilages is staged as T4 disease.
options.D: The most common site of nodal metastasis is the upper deep cervical group (level II).
options.E: It commonly sends distant metastasis to the lungs, bone and liver.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Smoking (with alcohol) is the major carcinogenic risk factor for laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, so this statement is true.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The subglottis is the least common primary site; most laryngeal squamous cell carcinomas are glottic or supraglottic, so 'seldom arises from the subglottic area' is true.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Invasion of the laryngeal cartilage is indeed staged as T4 disease, so this statement is correct.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The upper deep cervical (level II) nodes are the commonest site of nodal metastasis, so this is true.
explanations.E: Correct. Laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma is predominantly a locoregional disease, so distant metastasis is relatively UNCOMMON, and saying it 'commonly' spreads to lungs, bone and liver is the false statement. When distant spread does occur the lung is the usual site, but it is not a frequent event. The other four statements are all true.

questions.learning_objective: State that laryngeal SCC is mainly locoregional and that distant metastasis is uncommon.

questions.title: Purpose of CT in a fixed vocal cord tumour
questions.question: A 60-year-old man, a chronic heavy smoker, presents with hoarseness of several months, not responsive to medical treatment. Laryngeal examination shows a fungating mass arising from the right vocal cord, which is fixed. A CT scan in this case is indicated in order to determine:

options.A: The exact site of the tumour
options.B: The exact size of the tumour
options.C: Extension of the tumour to the hypopharynx
options.D: Extension of the tumour to the tongue base
options.E: Extension of the tumour to the cartilage and/or the intralaryngeal spaces

explanations.A: Incorrect. The exact site is already seen directly at laryngoscopy, so CT is not needed for that.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The surface size is assessed endoscopically; CT adds little just to measure the visible tumour.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hypopharyngeal extension is not the main question in a cord tumour that is already fixed; deep and cartilage spread is.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tongue-base extension is not the concern for a glottic tumour; it is a feature of very different sites.
explanations.E: Correct. In a fixed cord tumour, CT is done to reveal what the endoscope cannot see — invasion of the thyroid or cricoid cartilage and of the deep paraglottic and pre-epiglottic (intralaryngeal) spaces. This deep extension determines the T stage and whether cord-conserving surgery is possible. Cartilage invasion in particular upstages the tumour to T4.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that CT in a fixed cord tumour shows cartilage and deep-space invasion that guides staging and surgery.

questions.title: False statement about laryngeal leukoplakia
questions.question: All of the following are correct about leukoplakia of the larynx EXCEPT:

options.A: It is caused by excessive smoking.
options.C: It causes gradual hoarseness of voice.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Leukoplakia is strongly associated with heavy smoking, so this statement is true.
explanations.B: Correct. Leukoplakia is a premalignant lesion that CAN progress to squamous cell carcinoma through worsening dysplasia, so 'never turns malignant' is the false statement. It must be biopsied and followed up, and the patient advised to stop smoking. This malignant potential is exactly what makes it important.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A white patch on the vibrating cord causes gradual hoarseness, so this is a true statement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. By definition leukoplakia is a white plaque (from keratin), so this statement is true.

questions.learning_objective: State that leukoplakia is premalignant and can progress to carcinoma.

questions.title: Feature of the adult laryngeal papilloma
questions.question: Adult laryngeal papilloma is:

options.B: Arises from any part of the larynx.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The adult laryngeal papilloma is characteristically single (solitary); being multiple is a feature of the juvenile disease, not the adult lesion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The adult papilloma is a localised lesion usually sitting on the vocal cord, not one that arises from any part of the larynx (that describes the juvenile multiple form).
explanations.C: Incorrect. Spontaneous regression at puberty is a feature of the juvenile multiple papillomatosis, not of the adult papilloma.
explanations.D: Correct. The solitary adult laryngeal papilloma is regarded as premalignant, so it can undergo malignant change to squamous cell carcinoma. This is why it must be completely excised by microlaryngeal surgery and sent for histology. It contrasts with the multiple juvenile papillomatosis, which is usually benign and regresses at puberty.

questions.learning_objective: State that the adult laryngeal papilloma is solitary and premalignant.

questions.title: Why glottic carcinoma has a better prognosis
questions.question: Prognosis of glottic carcinoma is better because:

options.B: It causes early hoarseness of voice.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Late stridor reflects advanced airway narrowing and would signal a worse, not a better, outlook; it is not the reason for the good prognosis.
explanations.B: Correct. A glottic (vocal cord) tumour disturbs cord vibration from the start, so it produces hoarseness early and brings the patient to attention while the cancer is still small and curable. Together with the sparse lymphatic drainage of the glottis (so nodal spread is late), this early warning gives glottic carcinoma its relatively good prognosis. Any hoarseness lasting more than 2-3 weeks in a smoker therefore needs laryngoscopy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Absence of dysphagia is not the mechanism of the good prognosis; the key factor is that hoarseness appears early and the glottis has poor lymphatics.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Lymphatic metastasis worsens prognosis; in fact the glottis has poor lymphatics, so nodal spread is late, which is one reason the outlook is good.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that early hoarseness and poor glottic lymphatics give glottic carcinoma a good prognosis.

questions.title: Feature of multiple laryngeal papillomata
questions.question: Multiple papillomata of the larynx:

options.A: Do not extend beyond the vocal fold.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Multiple (juvenile) papillomatosis is not confined to the vocal fold; it can spread along the whole respiratory tract, affecting the supraglottis, subglottis and trachea.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The multiple juvenile papillomatosis is usually benign and rarely undergoes malignant change; malignant potential is the hallmark of the solitary adult papilloma, not the multiple juvenile form (see this bank's Q29 and Q31, where malignant transformation is the false statement for the children's disease).
explanations.C: Incorrect. As the lesions enlarge they cause not only hoarseness but also stridor and airway obstruction, so 'hoarseness only' is untrue.
explanations.D: Correct. Multiple laryngeal papillomatosis is the juvenile disease, and its classic natural history is a tendency to regress around puberty. The lesions are HPV-driven, multiple and recurrent, so they are managed by repeated microlaryngeal or laser excision to keep the airway clear until they regress. This benign, self-limiting behaviour distinguishes it from the premalignant solitary adult papilloma.

questions.learning_objective: State that multiple juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis is usually benign and regresses at puberty.

questions.title: Laryngeal cancer causing early stridor before hoarseness
questions.question: Causes early stridor before hoarseness of voice:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glottic carcinoma arises on the vocal cord, so it causes hoarseness EARLY and stridor only late, the opposite of the stem.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Epiglottic (supraglottic) carcinoma tends to present with throat discomfort, dysphagia and later a neck node, not with early stridor before hoarseness.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Supraglottic carcinoma is clinically silent early and usually presents late with throat symptoms or nodal disease, not with early stridor.
explanations.D: Correct. Subglottic carcinoma grows in the narrowest part of the larynx below the cords, so it obstructs the airway and causes stridor EARLY, while the vocal cords are spared until late, so hoarseness comes later. This late hoarseness means subglottic tumours are often diagnosed late. It is the reverse of glottic cancer, where hoarseness is the early warning sign.

questions.learning_objective: State that subglottic carcinoma causes early stridor with hoarseness appearing late.

questions.title: Nature of the adult laryngeal papilloma
questions.question: Laryngeal papilloma of adults is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The adult papilloma is single (solitary); being multiple describes the juvenile disease.
explanations.B: Correct. The adult solitary laryngeal papilloma is premalignant and can transform into squamous cell carcinoma, so it must be excised and examined histologically. It sits typically on the vocal cord and causes hoarseness. This premalignant potential is the key difference from the benign multiple juvenile papillomatosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Spontaneous cure (regression at puberty) belongs to the juvenile form; the adult lesion does not resolve on its own and needs excision.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A single cord papilloma causes hoarseness, not early stridor; airway obstruction with stridor is a feature of the bulky multiple juvenile disease.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the adult laryngeal papilloma as a solitary premalignant lesion.

questions.title: Earliest symptom of glottic carcinoma
questions.question: The earliest symptom of glottis carcinoma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Stridor appears only late, when the tumour has enlarged enough to narrow the airway; it is not the earliest symptom of glottic cancer.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dysphagia is a feature of hypopharyngeal or advanced supraglottic disease, not an early symptom of a glottic tumour.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cough is a non-specific late feature, not the earliest warning of glottic carcinoma.
explanations.D: Correct. A glottic carcinoma sits on the vibrating edge of the vocal cord, so it disturbs the voice from the outset, making progressive hoarseness the earliest symptom. This early warning allows detection while the tumour is small and gives glottic cancer its good prognosis. Persistent hoarseness beyond 2-3 weeks in a smoker mandates laryngoscopy.

questions.learning_objective: State that hoarseness is the earliest symptom of glottic carcinoma.

questions.title: Correct description of the adult laryngeal papilloma
questions.question: Adult papilloma of the larynx is:

options.A: Single and infiltrating the basement membrane.
options.D: Arises from any part of the larynx.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The adult papilloma is single but it is a surface (benign-appearing) lesion; infiltration through the basement membrane would already mean invasive carcinoma, not a papilloma.
explanations.B: Correct. The adult laryngeal papilloma is a solitary (single) lesion that is precancerous, so it can progress to squamous cell carcinoma and must be excised and examined histologically. It usually arises on the vocal cord and causes hoarseness. Being single and premalignant is exactly what separates it from the benign multiple juvenile disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Being multiple and large describes the juvenile papillomatosis, not the single adult lesion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Arising from any part of the larynx is a feature of the widespread juvenile disease; the adult papilloma is a localised solitary lesion, typically on the cord.

questions.learning_objective: Describe the adult laryngeal papilloma as single and precancerous.

questions.title: The precancerous laryngeal lesion among benign lesions
questions.question: One of the following laryngeal lesions is precancerous:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A singer's (vocal) nodule is a benign response to voice abuse with no malignant potential.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Laryngoscleroma is a chronic granulomatous infection that causes subglottic stenosis, not malignant transformation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Multiple (juvenile) papillomatosis is usually benign and only rarely turns malignant, so it is not the established premalignant lesion here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A laryngeal web is a congenital or acquired membrane between the cords; it causes voice and airway problems but is not premalignant.
explanations.E: Correct. The single (solitary adult) papilloma is the precancerous lesion in this list, as it can undergo malignant change to squamous cell carcinoma. It is therefore excised and sent for histology, and the patient is followed up. This premalignant potential distinguishes the solitary adult papilloma from the benign multiple juvenile disease.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the single adult papilloma as the premalignant lesion among benign laryngeal lesions.

questions.title: Typical patient with vocal cord carcinoma
questions.question: Carcinoma of the vocal cord is common in:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Young age is against laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma, which follows decades of exposure to tobacco.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is uncommon in the young and, historically, less common in females who smoked less.
explanations.C: Correct. Laryngeal (vocal cord) squamous cell carcinoma is a disease of ELDERLY MALES, because it is driven by long-term smoking and alcohol, exposures traditionally commonest in older men. It typically presents in the sixth and seventh decades. Rising female smoking is narrowing this sex difference, but the classic patient remains an elderly male smoker.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Elderly women are affected less often than elderly men, reflecting historically lower smoking rates.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Squamous cell carcinoma essentially does not occur in children; a warty laryngeal lesion in a child is juvenile papillomatosis, not carcinoma.

questions.learning_objective: State that laryngeal carcinoma is commonest in elderly male smokers.

questions.title: The wrong statement about laryngeal papilloma in children
questions.question: Laryngeal papilloma in children is: (One answer is wrong)

options.B: Arises at any site in the larynx.

explanations.A: Incorrect (a true statement). Childhood (juvenile) laryngeal papillomatosis is characteristically multiple, so this is correct, not the wrong one.
explanations.B: Incorrect (a true statement). The lesions can arise at any site in the larynx and along the respiratory tract, so this is true.
explanations.C: Correct. This is the wrong statement: the childhood (juvenile) papillomatosis is usually benign and does NOT typically show malignant transformation. Malignant potential is instead the hallmark of the solitary adult papilloma. So attributing malignant change to the children's disease is the false option here.
explanations.D: Incorrect (a true statement). Regression around puberty is the classic natural history of the juvenile disease, so this is true.
explanations.E: Incorrect (a true statement). A hormonal influence at puberty is invoked to explain the tendency to regress, so this is regarded as true.

questions.learning_objective: State that juvenile laryngeal papillomatosis is usually benign and does not typically turn malignant.

questions.hold: Exact in-source duplicate of Q19. Same stem ('All the following are correct about leukoplakia EXCEPT'), same four options (a caused by excessive smoking / b never turns malignant / c causes hoarseness / d white in colour) and the same printed key b (never turns malignant). Q19 was already authored, so Q30 is held so the identical item is not authored twice.

questions.title: The wrong statement about multiple laryngeal papillomata
questions.question: Multiple papillomata of larynx is characterized by the following EXCEPT:

options.C: Affects any part of larynx and trachea.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The multiple juvenile papillomatosis is characteristically recurrent, regrowing after removal, so this statement is true.
explanations.B: Incorrect. It is the disease of children (juvenile onset), so this is true.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The papillomas can affect any part of the larynx and extend into the trachea, so this is a true statement.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the exception: the multiple juvenile papillomatosis is usually benign and does NOT commonly turn malignant. Frequent malignant change is a feature of the solitary adult papilloma, not the juvenile multiple disease. So 'commonly turns malignant' is the false statement.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Because the lesions recur and threaten the airway, treatment is by repeated microlaryngeal or laser excision, so this statement is true.

questions.learning_objective: State that multiple juvenile papillomatosis is recurrent, treated by repeated excision, and does not commonly turn malignant.

questions.title: Which laryngeal lesion is precancerous
questions.question: The following lesion of the larynx is precancerous:

explanations.A: Correct. The single papilloma of the adult is the precancerous lesion here, as it can undergo malignant change to squamous cell carcinoma. It is therefore excised and sent for histology and the patient followed up. Its premalignant potential distinguishes it from the benign multiple juvenile disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Multiple (juvenile) laryngeal papillomatosis is usually benign and only rarely turns malignant, so it is not the premalignant lesion here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A singer's (vocal) nodule is a benign voice-abuse lesion with no malignant potential.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Laryngomalacia is a congenital softening of the supraglottic cartilage; it is not a neoplastic or premalignant lesion at all.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the single adult papilloma as the premalignant laryngeal lesion.

questions.title: Commonest site of a vocal cord nodule
questions.question: Most common location in the vocal cord of a vocal nodule:

explanations.A: Correct. Vocal (singer's) nodules form at the junction of the anterior one-third and the posterior two-thirds of the membranous vocal cord. This is the point of maximum vibratory contact and impact during phonation, so repeated voice abuse traumatises the mucosa there. Nodules are therefore typically bilateral and symmetrical at this site.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The anterior commissure is where the cords meet in front; it is not the site of maximal vibratory impact where nodules form.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The junction of the posterior one-third and anterior two-thirds (the point two-thirds from the front) is not the maximal-impact point; the nodule forms one-third from the front.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The posterior commissure is the cartilaginous (respiratory) part of the glottis, not the membranous vibrating segment where nodules arise.

questions.learning_objective: State that vocal cord nodules form at the junction of the anterior one-third and posterior two-thirds of the cord.

questions.title: The false statement about vocal cord nodules
questions.question: The following statements about vocal cord nodules are true EXCEPT:

options.C: Can be treated conservatively by voice therapy.
options.D: If not treated may present late by respiratory distress.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vocal nodules are caused by voice abuse or misuse (singers, teachers, screaming children), so this statement is true.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sitting on the vibrating cord, nodules cause hoarseness (and voice fatigue), so this is a true statement.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Early nodules are managed conservatively with voice therapy and voice rest, so this is true.
explanations.D: Correct. This is the false statement: vocal nodules are small mucosal swellings that do not obstruct the airway, so they do NOT present with respiratory distress even if untreated. They cause a persistent hoarse voice, not airway obstruction. Stridor and respiratory distress point instead to a bulky or obstructing lesion such as papillomatosis or a tumour.

questions.learning_objective: State that vocal nodules cause hoarseness treated by voice therapy and do not cause airway obstruction.

questions.title: Febrile child with stridor and respiratory distress
questions.question: A 5-year-old boy was brought to the emergency room with obvious stridor. His temperature was 38 degrees C. On examination the boy was clearly distressed, with retraction of the intercostal spaces and the suprasternal notch. The most probable diagnosis is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Laryngomalacia presents in early infancy with stridor and a normal voice, is not febrile, and would not first appear as acute distress at 5 years of age.
explanations.B: Incorrect. An inhaled foreign body causes SUDDEN choking without fever; the temperature of 38 degrees points to an infective cause instead.
explanations.C: Correct. A young child with fever, stridor and respiratory distress with intercostal and suprasternal retraction is the classic picture of acute laryngo-tracheo-bronchitis (viral croup). The narrow subglottis swells with the infection, so airflow becomes obstructed and noisy. It is the commonest infective cause of stridor in this age group and is managed with humidified oxygen, steroids and nebulised adrenaline.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Laryngeal diphtheria can cause febrile stridor but is now rare and is distinguished by a greyish pharyngeal pseudomembrane and marked toxaemia, making viral croup the far more probable diagnosis here.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) as the commonest cause of febrile stridor in a young child.

questions.title: Commonest laryngeal site in laryngoscleroma
questions.question: The most common laryngeal site of involvement in laryngoscleroma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The true vocal cords are not the predilection site; scleroma characteristically involves the subglottis.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The epiglottis is not the usual laryngeal site of scleroma.
explanations.C: Correct. Laryngoscleroma (the laryngeal extension of rhinoscleroma) most commonly affects the SUBGLOTTIS. Chronic granulomatous infiltration and later fibrosis there produce subglottic narrowing and stenosis. This subglottic predilection is why the disease presents with progressive stridor and hoarseness.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The arytenoids are not the characteristic site; the subglottis is the commonest laryngeal location of scleroma.

questions.learning_objective: State that laryngoscleroma most commonly involves the subglottis.

questions.title: Commonest presentation of laryngoscleroma
questions.question: The commonest presentation of laryngoscleroma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Scleroma is a submucosal granulomatous and fibrotic process; it narrows the subglottis rather than paralysing the cords.
explanations.B: Correct. Because laryngoscleroma affects the subglottis and causes progressive narrowing, its commonest presentation is stridor together with hoarseness of voice. The stridor reflects the fixed subglottic stenosis, and the hoarseness reflects involvement of the glottic region. This slowly progressive airway obstruction is characteristic of the fibrotic stage.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pain and night sweating are constitutional/infective symptoms (e.g. tuberculosis), not the typical presentation of scleroma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Scleroma is a benign chronic infection, not a malignancy, so it does not present with a metastatic lymph node.

questions.learning_objective: State that laryngoscleroma commonly presents with stridor and hoarseness.

questions.title: Why acute laryngitis is more dangerous in children
questions.question: Acute non-specific laryngitis in young children is more dangerous than in adults because it may cause:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hoarseness occurs in adults too and is not itself dangerous; it is not the reason laryngitis is more serious in children.
explanations.B: Correct. A young child's larynx, especially the subglottis, has a very narrow lumen and loose submucosa, so the mucosal swelling of acute laryngitis quickly narrows the airway and causes STRIDOR and obstruction. The same degree of oedema that is trivial in a wide adult airway can be life-threatening in a child. This is why laryngitis (and croup) is far more dangerous in children.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bronchopneumonia is a lower respiratory complication, not the reason laryngeal inflammation is dangerous at the level of the larynx in children.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aspiration is not the characteristic danger of childhood laryngitis; airway narrowing with stridor is.

questions.learning_objective: Explain that acute laryngitis is dangerous in children because the narrow airway obstructs and causes stridor.

questions.title: Site affected by laryngoscleroma
questions.question: Laryngoscleroma affects:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The epiglottis (a supraglottic structure) is not the characteristic site of scleroma.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The vocal cords (glottis) are not the main site; scleroma has a subglottic predilection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The region above the cords (supraglottis) is not the typical site of laryngeal scleroma.
explanations.D: Correct. Laryngoscleroma characteristically affects the region BELOW the vocal cords, i.e. the subglottis. Chronic granulomatous infiltration and fibrosis there cause subglottic stenosis with progressive stridor. This subglottic involvement is consistent with the disease's commonest laryngeal site being the subglottis.

questions.learning_objective: State that laryngoscleroma affects the subglottis (below the vocal cords).

questions.title: Causes of laryngeal perichondritis
questions.question: Perichondritis of the larynx may be caused by:

explanations.A: Incorrect as the single answer. A cut-throat wound exposes and infects the laryngeal cartilage and can cause perichondritis, but it is only one of the listed causes.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the single answer. A high tracheostomy that injures the cricoid can lead to perichondritis, but again this is only one cause.
explanations.C: Incorrect as the single answer. Radiotherapy to the larynx impairs cartilage vascularity and can cause (radio)perichondritis and necrosis, but it is only one of the causes.
explanations.D: Correct. All of the listed factors can cause laryngeal perichondritis: external trauma (a cut-throat wound), surgical injury to cartilage (a high tracheostomy damaging the cricoid), and radiotherapy that devitalises the cartilage. Each exposes or devitalises the perichondrium and cartilage so that infection sets in. Hence 'all of the above' is correct.

questions.learning_objective: List trauma, high tracheostomy and radiotherapy as causes of laryngeal perichondritis.

questions.title: The condition that does not cause laryngeal perichondritis
questions.question: Perichondritis of the larynx may be caused by the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct. Laryngomalacia is the exception: it is a congenital softening of the supraglottic cartilage in infants and does NOT cause perichondritis. Perichondritis follows something that infects or devitalises the cartilage. Laryngomalacia involves neither infection nor cartilage injury, so it is not a cause.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A cut-throat wound exposes and infects the laryngeal cartilage and is a genuine cause of perichondritis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A high tracheostomy can injure the cricoid cartilage and cause perichondritis, so it is a real cause.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cancer of the larynx (and its radiotherapy) can invade or devitalise cartilage and lead to perichondritis, so it is a genuine cause.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that laryngomalacia does not cause laryngeal perichondritis.

questions.title: Nerve of referred otalgia in laryngitis
questions.question: Laryngitis causes referred otalgia through:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The trigeminal (auriculotemporal) nerve refers otalgia from the teeth and temporomandibular joint, not from the larynx.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The glossopharyngeal nerve refers otalgia from the tonsil, oropharynx and posterior tongue, not from the larynx.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The great auricular nerve is a cervical-plexus sensory nerve to the skin over the parotid and lower ear; it does not carry referred pain from the larynx.
explanations.D: Correct. The larynx is supplied by the vagus nerve (through its superior and recurrent laryngeal branches), and the vagus also sends the auricular branch (Arnold's nerve) to the external ear. Because both share the vagal sensory pathway, laryngeal disease such as laryngitis or laryngeal cancer refers pain to the ear through the vagus. This is why persistent otalgia with a normal ear should prompt examination of the larynx.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The lesser occipital nerve supplies the scalp behind the ear and has no role in referred otalgia from the larynx.

questions.learning_objective: State that laryngeal disease refers otalgia to the ear through the vagus nerve (Arnold's nerve).

questions.title: The condition that does not cause subglottic stenosis
questions.question: Subglottic stenosis could occur as a result of any of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A congenital subglottic stenosis (a narrow cricoid ring from birth) is a recognised cause, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Rhinolaryngoscleroma causes subglottic granulomatous fibrosis and stenosis, so it is a genuine cause.
explanations.C: Correct. Leukoplakia is the exception: it is a white premalignant patch of the vocal cord mucosa and does NOT produce subglottic stenosis. Subglottic stenosis comes from processes that scar or narrow the subglottic ring (congenital, scleroma, prolonged intubation, cricoid injury). A surface mucosal patch on the cord is not one of them.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Prolonged endotracheal intubation is one of the commonest acquired causes of subglottic stenosis, from mucosal pressure necrosis and scarring, so it is a real cause.
explanations.E: Incorrect. A high tracheostomy that injures the cricoid cartilage leads to subglottic stenosis, so it is a genuine cause.

questions.learning_objective: List the causes of subglottic stenosis and recognise that leukoplakia is not one.

questions.title: The life-threatening vocal cord palsy
questions.question: In vocal fold (cord) lesions, which of the following is life threatening:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Unilateral abductor paralysis leaves the other cord to abduct, so the airway is maintained and it is not life threatening (the voice may be near normal).
explanations.B: Correct. In bilateral abductor paralysis both cords cannot move apart and lie close to the midline (paramedian), so the airway is critically narrowed while the voice may be surprisingly good. This produces stridor and can cause fatal airway obstruction, so it is the life-threatening lesion and may need an emergency tracheostomy. It is the dangerous complication classically seen after total thyroidectomy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Unilateral adductor paralysis leaves a gap so the voice is breathy, but the airway is wide open, so it is not life threatening.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bilateral adductor paralysis leaves the cords abducted (apart): the airway is patent (no obstruction) though the patient has aphonia and a poor cough, so it is not immediately life threatening to the airway.

questions.learning_objective: State that bilateral abductor vocal cord paralysis is the life-threatening palsy because it obstructs the airway.

questions.title: The cause that does not give a hot potato voice
questions.question: Hot potato voice is caused by the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. A supraglottic carcinoma is a mass above the cords that muffles the voice, giving the hot potato quality, so it is a genuine cause.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute epiglottitis swells the supraglottis and produces the muffled hot potato voice, so it is a real cause.
explanations.C: Correct. Glottic carcinoma is the exception: because it sits on the vibrating vocal cord it causes HOARSENESS, not a hot potato voice. The muffled hot potato (plummy) voice comes from lesions ABOVE the cords in the supraglottis or oropharynx that impede resonance while the cords still vibrate. A tumour on the cord itself changes the voice to hoarse instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Marked tonsillar (or oropharyngeal) hypertrophy obstructs the oropharynx and muffles the voice, producing a hot potato voice, so it is a genuine cause.

questions.learning_objective: State that a hot potato voice comes from supraglottic/oropharyngeal lesions, not from glottic carcinoma.

questions.title: The condition that does not cause stridor
questions.question: Stridor is a characteristic feature of the following diseases EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Laryngeal diphtheria forms an obstructing membrane in the larynx and causes stridor, so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Angioneurotic (angioedema) oedema of the larynx swells the airway and causes stridor, so it is a genuine cause.
explanations.C: Correct. Adenoid hypertrophy is the exception: the adenoids sit in the nasopharynx, so their enlargement causes nasal obstruction, snoring and mouth-breathing, NOT stridor. Stridor is a sign of obstruction at the larynx or trachea, below the nasopharynx. Adenoidal obstruction produces a nasal, not a laryngeal, airway noise.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bilateral abductor vocal cord paralysis holds the cords near the midline and narrows the glottis, causing stridor, so it is a real cause.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that stridor is a laryngotracheal sign and that adenoid hypertrophy causes nasal obstruction, not stridor.

questions.hold: Non-unique definition stem. 'Stridor is:' is keyed d (difficult noisy breathing), but option b (noisy breathing) is an equally valid textbook definition of stridor, which is fundamentally a NOISE produced by turbulent airflow through a narrowed airway and does not by definition require breathing difficulty (mild/subclinical stridor exists). Two defensible options (b and d) make the key non-unique; held per the never-guess rule.

questions.title: The non-inflammatory cause of stridor
questions.question: Inflammatory causes of stridor include the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute epiglottitis is an acute bacterial inflammation of the supraglottis causing stridor, so it is an inflammatory cause.
explanations.B: Correct. Laryngomalacia is the exception: it is a CONGENITAL structural softening of the supraglottic cartilage, not an inflammatory disease. It causes stridor by collapse of the flaccid supraglottis on inspiration, not by inflammation. The other four options are all inflammatory/infective causes of stridor.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Laryngeal diphtheria is an infective (inflammatory) membranous laryngitis that causes stridor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Laryngosclerosis (scleroma) is a chronic granulomatous infection causing subglottic stenosis and stridor, so it is inflammatory in origin.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Laryngeal tuberculosis is a chronic infective inflammation of the larynx that can cause stridor.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish congenital laryngomalacia from the inflammatory/infective causes of stridor.

questions.title: The lesion that does not obstruct the paediatric airway
questions.question: The following are causes of paediatric airway obstruction EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Acute epiglottitis swells the supraglottis and can rapidly obstruct a child's airway, so it is a genuine cause.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) narrows the subglottis and is a common cause of paediatric airway obstruction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Recurrent respiratory papillomatosis produces bulky multiple cord papillomas that obstruct the airway, so it is a real cause.
explanations.D: Correct. A singer's (vocal) nodule is the exception: it is a tiny mucosal swelling on the cord that causes hoarseness but does NOT obstruct the airway, so it is not a cause of paediatric airway obstruction. Airway obstruction comes from bulky or swelling lesions (epiglottitis, croup, papillomatosis). A small nodule simply alters the voice.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a vocal nodule causes hoarseness but not airway obstruction.

questions.title: Feature of a high tracheostomy
questions.question: High tracheostomy:

options.A: Is usually done in emergency cases.
options.B: Has the risk of cricoid injury with subsequent subglottic stenosis.
options.D: Is done in the first two tracheal rings.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A high tracheostomy is not the routine emergency airway (that is cricothyroidotomy or a mid-level tracheostomy); it is specifically avoided because of its complications.
explanations.B: Correct. A high tracheostomy is placed too close to or through the first tracheal ring/cricoid, so it risks injuring the cricoid cartilage, and healing there causes subglottic stenosis. This is exactly why a high tracheostomy is condemned and the tube is normally placed through the second-to-third tracheal rings. The cricoid is the only complete ring of the airway, so damage to it narrows the subglottis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Speed and ease are not the defining feature and do not make it acceptable; the clinically important point is the cricoid-injury risk.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A standard (safe) tracheostomy is through the second and third rings; a high one is above this near the cricoid, so 'first two tracheal rings' does not correctly define it and is not the intended answer.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Because A, C and D are not correct, 'all of the above' cannot be the answer; the single correct statement is the cricoid-injury risk.

questions.learning_objective: State that a high tracheostomy risks cricoid injury and subsequent subglottic stenosis.

questions.title: Distress with a patent tracheostomy tube
questions.question: An 8-year-old boy had an urgent tracheostomy under local anaesthesia for stridor due to laryngeal papillomatosis. Immediately after surgery he became distressed with increased effort of breathing and intercostal retractions despite adequate air flow from the tracheostomy tube. The most likely event is:

options.A: Slipped tracheostomy tube out of the trachea.
options.B: Pneumothorax due to injury of the pleura.
options.D: Bilateral injury of the recurrent laryngeal nerves.
options.E: Occluded lumen of the tracheostomy tube with dry mucus crust.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A tube slipped out of the trachea would give NO or poor airflow through the tube, but the stem states airflow through the tube is adequate, so this is excluded.
explanations.B: Correct. Distress with retractions DESPITE a well-functioning tube means the problem is in the chest, not the tube. In a child the pleural dome rises high into the neck, so it can be injured during a low or difficult tracheostomy, causing a pneumothorax that gives respiratory distress even though the airway itself is patent. Urgent chest examination and a chest X-ray (and drainage) are needed.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Surgical emphysema causes neck swelling and crepitus but does not usually cause acute severe respiratory distress with retractions when the tube is working.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury affects the cords, but the airway is now bypassed by a patent tracheostomy tube, so it would not cause this post-operative distress.
explanations.E: Incorrect. An occluded (crusted) tube would reduce airflow through the tube, whereas the stem specifies airflow is adequate, so this is excluded.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise pneumothorax as the cause of post-tracheostomy distress when the tube airflow is adequate.

questions.title: The condition that is not an indication for tracheostomy
questions.question: The following are indications of tracheostomy EXCEPT:

options.A: Expected prolonged intubation in the intensive care unit.
options.B: Before resection of a large oro-mandibular cancer.
options.C: Extensive leukoplakia affecting both vocal cords.
options.D: Bilateral vocal cord paralysis after total thyroidectomy.
options.E: Advanced supraglottic laryngeal cancer obstructing the laryngeal inlet.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Anticipated prolonged ventilation/intubation is a standard indication for tracheostomy (to protect the larynx and ease weaning), so it is not the exception.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A tracheostomy is done to secure the airway before or during resection of a large oro-mandibular cancer, so it is a genuine indication.
explanations.C: Correct. Extensive leukoplakia of both cords is the exception: leukoplakia is a thin white mucosal (premalignant) patch that does not obstruct the airway, so it is not an indication for tracheostomy. Tracheostomy is indicated for actual or expected airway obstruction or prolonged ventilation, not for a surface mucosal lesion. The lesion is managed by biopsy and excision, not by tracheostomy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bilateral vocal cord paralysis after total thyroidectomy narrows the airway (cords near the midline) and is a classic indication for tracheostomy.
explanations.E: Incorrect. An advanced supraglottic cancer obstructing the laryngeal inlet needs a tracheostomy to secure the airway, so it is a genuine indication.

questions.learning_objective: List the indications for tracheostomy and recognise that extensive cord leukoplakia is not one.

questions.title: Why a high tracheostomy is bad
questions.question: High tracheostomy is bad because:

options.A: It may cause injury of the subclavian artery.
options.B: It may cause injury of the thyroid cartilage.
options.C: It may cause injury of the cricoid cartilage.
options.D: It may cause injury of the thyroid gland.

explanations.A: Incorrect. Subclavian artery injury is a risk of a LOW tracheostomy placed near the great vessels, not of a high one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The thyroid cartilage lies above the cricoid at the level of the vocal cords; a tracheostomy is not made through it, so it is not the reason a high tracheostomy is bad.
explanations.C: Correct. A high tracheostomy is bad because it is placed too close to or through the cricoid cartilage and can injure it. The cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring of the airway, so damage to it heals with scarring and subglottic stenosis. This is why the tube should be placed lower, through the second-to-third tracheal rings.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The thyroid gland isthmus is encountered at the mid-tracheal level of a standard tracheostomy, not specifically in a high one, so gland injury is not the defining fault of a high tracheostomy.

questions.learning_objective: State that a high tracheostomy is bad because it injures the cricoid cartilage and causes subglottic stenosis.

questions.title: Laser used in microlaryngosurgery
questions.question: The laser commonly used in microlaryngosurgery is:

explanations.A: Correct. The carbon dioxide (CO2) laser is the one commonly used in microlaryngeal surgery, because its beam is strongly absorbed by water in soft tissue, giving very precise, shallow cutting with minimal thermal spread to the surrounding cords. This precision suits delicate work such as excising papillomas or small cord lesions. It is coupled to the operating microscope for microlaryngoscopy.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The Nd:YAG laser penetrates deeply and is used for bulkier or vascular lesions (e.g. tracheobronchial tumours), not for precise cord microsurgery.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The argon laser is absorbed by pigment and is used mainly in ophthalmology and dermatology, not routinely for microlaryngosurgery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The KTP laser is used for some vascular and airway lesions, but the standard laser for microlaryngeal surgery is the CO2 laser.

questions.learning_objective: State that the CO2 laser is the laser commonly used in microlaryngosurgery.
